title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a pedagogically fine-tuned generative AI tutor (LearnLM) can safely and effectively support student learning in real secondary school classrooms, and how its performance compares with both static hints and human tutors. The central question is whether generative AI can help scale individualized tutoring without sacrificing safety or learning quality, given known risks such as hallucinations, poor pedagogy, or student frustration.

The intervention was implemented on the Eedi mathematics platform in chat-based one-to-one tutoring. In an exploratory randomized controlled trial, 165 students were randomly assigned either to receive static pre-written hints or interactive tutoring. For tutoring sessions, there was a second level of randomization: students were connected either to a human tutor alone or to LearnLM, whose every drafted message was reviewed by an expert human tutor before being sent. The study also included message audits, tutor surveys, student surveys, and semi-structured tutor interviews to assess safety, instructional quality, and user experience.

Participants were Year 9 and 10 students (ages 13–15) from five UK secondary schools, along with 17 expert tutors who were qualified teachers. The trial ran over seven consecutive weeks during regular mathematics instruction using the Eedi platform. The study context was classroom-based platform use for one hour per week, with support triggered when students answered the first question in a study unit incorrectly.

The main conclusion is that supervised AI tutoring was safe and at least as effective as human tutoring on the measured outcomes, and better than static hints. Tutors approved about three-quarters of LearnLM’s drafted messages with no edits, and post hoc review found zero harmful messages and very few factual errors. Students supported by LearnLM performed similarly to those with human tutors on immediate error correction and misconception resolution, and showed somewhat better transfer to subsequent topics. Tutors also reported that LearnLM was especially strong at generating Socratic questions and could improve efficiency, though human supervision remained important for pacing, tone, and social-emotional nuance. The authors caution that the findings are limited to short-term mathematics outcomes in a specific supervised setting and may not generalize to less structured subjects such as literature or history.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory randomized controlled trial conducted in real classrooms with N=165 students, which is stronger than correlational evidence. However, it is a recent non-peer-reviewed tech report with some limitations: supervised AI rather than autonomous deployment, short duration, session-level crossover, and no long-term standardized assessments.
impact_tier_rationale: The strongest reported advantage is a modest gain in knowledge transfer for LearnLM over human tutoring (+5.5 percentage points), with broad parity or modest benefits over comparators rather than large effects. Effects are promising but still uncertain and domain-specific to secondary mathematics, not literacy.

interventions.use_case: Pedagogically fine-tuned generative AI (LearnLM) drafts Socratic chat-based mathematics tutoring messages for UK secondary students, with each message reviewed and optionally edited by expert human tutors before delivery.
Static pre-written misconception-specific hints on the Eedi platform serve as a non-interactive digital support comparator against interactive tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory classroom RCT with N=165 UK secondary students, supervised LearnLM tutoring performed at least as well as human tutoring and better than static hints on math learning outcomes. Students with LearnLM support answered the immediate retry correctly 93.0% of the time (95% credible interval [90.4%, 95.3%]) versus 91.2% [88.5%, 93.6%] for human tutors and 65.4% [63.8%, 66.9%] for static hints; for transfer to the next topic, LearnLM reached 66.2% [61.1%, 71.2%] versus 60.7% [55.8%, 65.4%] for human tutors, a +5.5 percentage point difference with 95% credible interval [-1.4%, +12.4%] and 93.6% posterior probability of advantage.
finding.measure: Math performance on Eedi platform: mistake remediation (correct second attempt), misconception resolution (any correct response within unit), and knowledge transfer (correct first question in subsequent study unit)
finding.effect_size: +5.5 percentage points for knowledge transfer vs human tutoring; immediate success 93.0% vs 91.2% vs 65.4%
finding.confidence_interval: 95% credible interval for transfer difference vs human tutor: [-1.4%, +12.4%]; LearnLM transfer rate [61.1%, 71.2%]

finding.finding_summary: Static pre-written hints were less effective than interactive tutoring on all measured math outcomes, but still produced substantial rates of error correction and misconception resolution. Students receiving static hints solved the retry question correctly 65.4% of the time (95% credible interval [63.8%, 66.9%]), resolved misconceptions 86.8% [85.7%, 88.0%], and transferred to the next topic at 56.2% [54.2%, 58.2%], below both LearnLM-supported and human tutoring conditions.
finding.measure: Math performance on Eedi platform: immediate retry correctness, misconception resolution within unit, and next-unit knowledge transfer
finding.effect_size: Static hints: 65.4% immediate correction, 86.8% misconception resolution, 56.2% transfer
finding.confidence_interval: 95% credible intervals: immediate correction [63.8%, 66.9%], misconception resolution [85.7%, 88.0%], transfer [54.2%, 58.2%]

finding.finding_summary: Tutor reports and post-trial survey data suggest the AI-supported workflow improved tutoring efficiency and capacity, though the study did not rigorously measure throughput experimentally. Among tutors, 82.4% selected 'supporting multiple students at the same time' as LearnLM’s most useful feature, and the authors state the RCT design precluded causal efficiency estimation, so this should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive evidence.
finding.measure: Tutor surveys/interviews on workload, multitasking capacity, and perceived efficiency
finding.effect_size: 82.4% of tutors endorsed multitasking support as most useful feature

finding.finding_summary: Student and tutor experience data indicate generally positive perceived helpfulness alongside concerns about frustration and pacing. Students receiving interactive tutoring rated support 3.9 out of 5 versus 3.6 for static hints, with a 74.9% posterior probability of an advantage for tutoring, but tutors frequently edited LearnLM messages to avoid exasperating students and to add social-emotional nuance.
finding.measure: Student helpfulness surveys and tutor qualitative reports about engagement, frustration, tone, and pacing
finding.study_size: N=27 student survey responses; N=17 tutors; N=5 tutor interviews
finding.effect_size: Student helpfulness ratings 3.9/5 for interactive tutoring vs 3.6/5 for static hints
finding.confidence_interval: Student helpfulness for tutoring [3.1, 4.7]; static hints [2.9, 4.2]

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative evidence suggests LearnLM’s Socratic questioning may support deeper reflection and metacognitive engagement during problem solving. Tutors consistently praised the model’s tendency to ask probing questions and reported that students tutored by LearnLM showed better transfer to novel subsequent topics, though no direct validated measure of metacognition or critical thinking was administered.
finding.measure: Tutor interviews on Socratic dialogue and indirect evidence from transfer to subsequent math topics
finding.study_size: N=165 students for transfer outcome; N=5 tutor interviews
finding.effect_size: +5.5 percentage points in next-topic transfer vs human tutoring
finding.confidence_interval: 95% credible interval for transfer difference vs human tutor: [-1.4%, +12.4%]
